items.title: Binance gets an Abu Dhabi court order covering $2.85B in hack proceeds that third parties froze, and names Circle and WLFI
items.idea: ADGM Courts ordered 18 companies, Circle and World Liberty Financial among them, not to release, lend, swap or commingle tokens frozen after Binance's Oct. 29 hack. Binance puts the total frozen or intercepted at ~$2.85B. Tether says it froze ~$1.5B on its own and isn't on the list; Binance is dealing with Tether one-on-one. The injunction comes back to court on Dec. 1.
items.angle: Issuer freezes are now the main recovery tool after a hack, and a court order makes them enforceable. That cuts both ways for the 'censorship-resistant' story around $USDC, $USDT and WLFI's USD1.
items.tweetA: Tether froze ~$1.5B of Binance's hack proceeds on its own. That's around half of the $2.85B frozen in total, by one company, with no court involved. Stablecoins aren't bearer assets anymore. They're bank deposits with a nicer API.
items.tweetB: A court in Abu Dhabi just told Circle and the Trump family's WLFI what they can and can't do with tokens they hold. Watch Dec. 1. If the injunction holds, the 'issuer + court' recovery playbook becomes standard after every big hack.

items.title: Ledger's tampered-wallet implant has spread from SE Asia to Berlin and possibly Dubai
items.idea: Every confirmed device has the same physical modification, designed to capture the recovery phrase during setup. Ledger says its chips and software aren't flawed and no confirmed device was bought on ledger.com. It wants to hear from anyone who bought a Ledger in Berlin since January 2026 and expects more devices to turn up. Owners can send units to Vierzon, France, for X-ray inspection.
items.angle: This is a hardware supply-chain attack on self-custody: the reseller channel is the weak point. It supports direct-from-OEM distribution and MPC/multisig custody (BitGo, Anchorage, Bitkey).
items.tweetA: A Ledger bought from a reseller now needs an X-ray in France to be trusted. Self-custody now carries supply-chain risk, the same way chips do. Cold storage was meant to be the safe option.
items.tweetB: Same week: Ledger implants found in Berlin, malware slipped into 178 sites including Ledger's, and 64,000 mining rigs hijacked. Crypto's attack surface has moved from smart contracts to physical hardware and distribution.

items.title: Kalshi loses in the Fourth Circuit, and the two judges in the majority disagree on why
items.idea: The Fourth Circuit upheld the denial of Kalshi's preliminary injunction against Maryland's sports-wagering rules. Judge Gregory said gambling is a state matter even if the contracts are swaps. Judge Thacker said they aren't swaps at all. Judge Benjamin dissented, saying they are swaps. That makes 3 circuits against Kalshi (4th, 6th, 9th) and 1 for it (3rd).
items.angle: A 3-1 circuit split with a split majority is the setup for a Supreme Court case. Whether sports event contracts count as 'swaps' decides whether prediction markets get one federal regulator (the CFTC) or 50 state gaming regimes.
items.tweetA: Three judges gave three different answers to 'is a sports event contract a swap?' The circuits are 3-1 against Kalshi. This is heading to SCOTUS, and the answer decides whether prediction markets are a CFTC product or a state casino license.
items.tweetB: Hyperliquid's HIP-4 outcome markets are picking up just as Kalshi loses its third appeals court. Lose in the federal courts and the volume moves onchain.

items.title: Leipzig judge offers to drop charges against the Movie2k defendant if he hands over 40,000 BTC (~€2.5B)
items.idea: The proposal: drop tax-evasion and money-laundering charges if the main Movie2k defendant gives up 40,000 BTC and pays €38M to victims. Investigators say he still holds ~56,000 BTC. A hearing is set for Dec. 3.
items.angle: If this goes through, Germany could end up with another large BTC pile to sell, and the 2024 Saxony sales are the template. With BTC under $63k and the daily RSI below 20, a known seller is the last thing the market needs.
items.tweetA: €2.5B for 40,000 BTC works out to about €62.5k per coin. If he takes the deal he keeps ~16,000 BTC, roughly €1B. A German state ends up holding 40k BTC. Last time Saxony had a pile like that, it sold it at the bottom.
items.tweetB: A criminal case settled in bitcoin. The prosecutor is in effect offering a plea priced in BTC. Whatever you think of that, the supply question for BTC in early 2027 just got bigger.

items.title: HKMA floats an onchain AI agent for crypto AML: $150B in illicit flows, 84% of it in stablecoins
items.idea: Hong Kong's bank regulator described an onchain AI agent that would combine blockchain analytics, KYC data and scam intelligence to speed up AML checks and fund freezes. It gave no rule or timeline. HKMA enforcement chief Raymond Chan cited Chainalysis: more than $150B in illicit crypto flows last year, 84% of them in stablecoins.
items.angle: If 84% of illicit flow runs through stablecoins, regulators will go after issuers and freeze tooling, not BTC. That ties directly to the Binance/Tether freezes.
items.tweetA: $150B of illicit crypto flow, 84% of it in stablecoins. Regulators are going to build their AML around freezable dollar tokens, not bitcoin. Stablecoin issuers are turning into compliance utilities.
items.tweetB: Hong Kong wants an AI agent that can freeze funds onchain at machine speed. Pair that with Fed Governor Barr warning about AI agents causing bank runs the same week. Regulators want agents for themselves and limits on agents for everyone else.

items.title: ETH staking yield is down to ~2.2%, while the US 10y yields 5.11%
items.idea: A Kairos Research, Golem Foundation and Ethereum Institutional report says ETH staking yields have fallen to about 2.2% and asks what ETH treasury companies can do beyond staking.
items.angle: The 10y is at 5.11% (Bespoke). Holding staked ETH now gives up ~290bp against Treasuries, which strains the ETH treasury-company model (BitMine holds 4.97% of supply).
items.tweetA: ETH staking pays 2.2%. The 10y pays 5.11%. You now give up ~290bp a year to hold 'productive' ETH instead of T-bills. The ETH-as-bond pitch only works when rates are low.
items.tweetB: BitMine holds 4.97% of all ETH and the staking yield is 2.2%. When 'what can treasuries do beyond staking?' turns into a sponsored research report, the yield story has run out.

items.title: Plumbing roundup: Visa stablecoin prefunding in APAC, senators press Treasury on GENIUS, Two Prime 5-year alt-collateral loans
items.idea: Visa is piloting stablecoin prefunding for Visa Direct cross-border payouts in APAC with dtcpay, after going into US production in October. Six senators led by Lummis and Gillibrand asked Treasury to extend the GENIUS safe harbor to state-licensed issuers, warning the draft pushes issuers toward federal charters. Two Prime now lends for up to five years against ETH, SOL, HYPE, XRP, ZEC, AVAX and tokenized gold, after originating more than $4B in BTC-backed loans since 2024.
items.angle: Stablecoins are being wired into existing card rails (Visa) faster than the regulatory perimeter is being settled. Five-year credit against altcoins is a late-cycle credit signal.
items.tweetA: Visa now prefunds cross-border payouts with stablecoins in the US and APAC. The killer app turned out to be treasury management for a card network, not payments.
items.tweetB: Five-year loans against HYPE and ZEC, while XRP is down 36% this quarter. Either crypto credit has matured a lot, or someone's collateral haircut assumptions are about to get tested.

items.title: Bullish Q3: adjusted net income +35% while digital asset sales fall 23%, plus a $300M buyback
items.idea: Bullish reported Q3 adjusted net income of $18.7M, up 35% YoY, while digital asset sales fell 23% to $32.1B. The board authorized buybacks of up to $300M. Its Equiniti acquisition should close in January 2027.
items.angle: Profit rising while volume falls means the exchange is diversifying away from trading fees, and buying Equiniti (a transfer agent) is a bet on tokenized securities.
items.tweetA: Bullish's volume fell 23% and its profit rose 35%. Crypto exchanges are learning to make money without a bull market, and buying a transfer agent (Equiniti) says where they think the next fees are.
items.tweetB: Kraken buys a VC firm ($2.7B AUM Tribe), Bullish buys a transfer agent, and Variational raises at $1.5B in a bear tape. Crypto firms are using this drawdown to buy pieces of TradFi.

items.title: K3 Capital's sBOLD vault drained of $3.43M via a self-liquidation flash-loan loop
items.idea: Per Blockaid, attackers used a wstETH flash loan to liquidate their own Liquity V2 trove, mint sBOLD shares cheaply and redeem other depositors' BOLD. K3 paused the contracts.
items.angle: Yield vaults built on top of other protocols inherit the base protocol's edge cases. Composability risk is still the main DeFi tail risk.
items.tweetA: The attacker liquidated themselves on purpose to get underpriced vault shares. In DeFi, your own liquidation can be the exploit. $3.43M is the price of an oracle and share-price assumption nobody stress-tested.
items.tweetB: Staking pays 2.2%, so vaults reach for yield by stacking protocols, and each layer adds an edge case like this one. Low base yields push DeFi toward this kind of risk.

items.title: Kraken's parent buys Tribe Capital ($2.7B AUM), a VC firm chaired by Kraken's own co-CEO
items.idea: Payward agreed to acquire Tribe Capital, which has $2.7B under management and was co-founded and is chaired by Kraken co-CEO Arjun Sethi. Terms weren't disclosed; closing is expected in Q1 2027.
items.angle: It's a related-party deal ahead of a likely Kraken listing. It gives Kraken an in-house venture arm, but governance-minded investors will look hard at the price.
items.tweetA: Kraken is buying the VC firm its own co-CEO co-founded and chairs, terms undisclosed, right before a likely IPO. Expect the S-1 to spend a lot of words on this.
items.tweetB: Exchanges keep turning into conglomerates: Kraken plus a VC fund, Bullish plus a transfer agent, Coinbase plus Morpho lending. Crypto is rebuilding the universal bank from the exchange outward.

items.title: S&P 500 vs Consumer Staples ratio is rolling over, the same signal it gave at the GFC, 2015-16, 2018 and COVID
items.idea: De Pablos plots SPX relative to Staples against SPX itself. The ratio has tended to lead at major turning points (GFC, 2015–16, 2018, COVID) and is now rolling over again, which suggests defensive leadership is taking hold. 'If that black line continues lower, look out below.'
items.angle: Read it alongside Waller's 50bp hike talk and the 10y at 5.11%. Staples leading in a hiking cycle with weak claims and Philly Fed points to a late-cycle rotation. The pair to watch is long $XLP / short $QQQ.
items.tweetA: The S&P/Staples ratio turned before the GFC, 2015, 2018 and COVID, and it's turning now. In a market where everyone's arguing about ANT's first day, toothpaste and cigarettes are quietly leading.
items.tweetB: You'd expect Staples to suffer at a 5.11% 10y, since they're bond proxies. They're outperforming anyway. When bond proxies beat growth while yields rise, the market is pricing a hit to earnings, not to multiples.

items.title: Pinkert: Dr. Copper 'jumped out the hospital window' and is signalling recession, with a $4.70 target
items.idea: Dale Pinkert says the huge red candle on copper 'doesn't look like any kind of bottom' and sees $4.70 or lower. He says copper is now 'telling you there's going to be a recession.' His seasonal frame: 'the bears feast on Thanksgiving and the bulls on Christmas', so a washout into Thanksgiving could set up a turn.
items.angle: Copper is breaking down at the same time Goldman's copper team (earlier today) and Haymaker talk about deficits. A price falling despite a deficit is a dollar and demand-destruction story, with $FCX already capitulating (Sinn).
items.tweetA: Copper is in a supply deficit and still crashing. When the deficit story stops supporting the price, the market is telling you demand is breaking faster than supply. That's the recession signal.
items.tweetB: Copper to $4.70, the dollar at its highest since April 2025, and Waller wanting 50bp. Dr. Copper isn't sick; the strong dollar is pushing it down.

items.title: Pinkert's metals levels: gold $3,800 to prove a bottom, silver $50 above / $43.50 below (or $34)
items.idea: Pinkert likes gold's current range but sees no evidence of a bottom; $3,800 is the level that would prove it's more than a bear-market rally. He made an unleveraged silver purchase but says $50 is the key level up top. A break of $43.50 would mean 'metals done for a year' and $34 silver.
items.angle: These are clear lines for metals risk. With real yields rising, the $43.50 silver level is the one that matters for $SLV and miners ($SIL).
items.tweetA: Silver's tell is $43.50. Below it, Pinkert sees $34, which is another -22%. A trader buying spot silver with no leverage while calling for $34 tells you how two-sided this tape is.
items.tweetB: Gold needs $3,800 just to prove it isn't a bear-market rally. Gold was the 2025 trade everyone owned, and in 2026 it's the one people are selling to meet margin.

items.title: Pinkert: the 10y hit his 5.10–5.15% target and is rolling over; long EUR/short CHF, short CAD, bearish JPY
items.idea: 'I said the 10 year would get up to 5.10-5.15%. Bingo. Failing rally.' He thinks yields are heading down. On the dollar he's 'probing for a top': the daily is diverging but the 4-hour isn't, so it could retest $104. items.tweetB: Bearish the yen because it's correlated to rates, while calling the top in rates. If US yields roll over, the yen short is the crowded trade that breaks first. $USDJPY

items.source: The Market House / Maggie Lake (Dale Pinkert)
items.title: Pinkert: 'Everyone loved high yield, that's changed.' He sees HY spreads blowing out and new lows in HYG
items.idea: 'What a difference six months makes... You're going to see credit spreads continue to blow out. We're going to make new lows in HYG.' He also keeps strong conviction that banks and $IGV (software) are sells.
items.angle: Pair this with Capital Flows' call that we've left the 'credit cycle melt-up' and with Moody's cutting Nvidia's outlook. Short $HYG and short $KRE fit together as late-cycle trades.
items.tweetA: Six months ago HY was the consensus carry trade. Now Pinkert wants new lows in $HYG, Capital Flows says the credit melt-up is over, and the Fed's stability report names AI financing as a top risk. Credit is where the AI unwind shows up next.
items.tweetB: Banks and software are his two highest-conviction shorts. Software is the sector AI is supposed to disrupt, and banks lend against everything else. Short $IGV / short $KBE is the 'AI wins, incumbents lose' trade with leverage.

items.source: The Market House / Maggie Lake (Dale Pinkert)
items.title: Pinkert: NVDA needs to reclaim $170; an SPX washout to 7,000-7,200 'takes everything with it,' including Apple
items.idea: Despite strong earnings and raised guidance, NVDA is still falling. 'To get really bullish it would have to recapture $170... too early to buy, maybe a little late to short.' Amazon is one of the stronger names, but he's neutral. Intel overshot his $60 target. Hiding places like Apple could be next to get hit.
items.angle: This lines up with Capital Flows' 7,400 line and ES at 7,227. The flush may have most of the way left to his 7,000 level, about 3% lower.
items.tweetA: NVDA beat and raised and is still making new lows. When good news can't lift the leader, the market is pricing the CEO, the financing and the cycle rather than the quarter.
items.tweetB: If SPX flushes to 7,000, the last shoe is Apple, the stock people hide in. When the place people hide starts falling, that's usually close to the bottom.

items.title: Waller calls for a 50bp hike in December to reverse the 'insurance cuts' made since summer 2025
items.idea: Waller, who has grown more hawkish since Warsh became Fed Chair, argued that consumers are starting to expect 3% inflation and that this can become self-fulfilling. He said the Fed should hike 50bp in December and reverse the insurance cuts made since summer 2025. That poured fuel on a dollar rally now at its highest since April 2025 and caused 'a bloodbath in commodities.'
items.angle: A 50bp hike floated by a Governor in a market already down 30% from highs (NVDA) is a policy-error setup. Watch the December SOFR futures and $DXY.
items.tweetA: Fed Governor Waller wants to hike 50bp in December while jobless claims and the Philly Fed both miss. Hiking into weakening data to fight 3% inflation expectations is how 2026 turns into 1994, or 2008.
items.tweetB: Waller kneecaps commodities, ANT lifts tech, and the dollar is at its highest since April 2025. The Fed is now the main driver of commodity prices, not supply and demand. Copper's 'recession signal' may just be a dollar signal.

items.title: Even after the ANT-day rally, the Nasdaq 100 is still ~1% below its 200-DMA; 10y at 5.11%; Japan machinery orders miss
items.idea: Nasdaq futures were +2% and SPX +1% on the Anthropic debut, but NDX would still open ~1% below its 200-DMA. The 10y is up 4bp to 5.11%, oil +1%, gold -0.6%, BTC +2%. Hong Kong fell 2% on potential China tech restrictions. Japan machinery orders fell 0.3% versus +1.3% expected. Philly Fed and claims both came in weaker than expected.
items.angle: A bounce driven by the IPO, under the 200-DMA, with the long end selling off, is a weak signal. Bulltard and Capital Flows both said the move faded by midday.
items.tweetA: The biggest IPO in history and the Nasdaq still can't get back over its 200-DMA. The market is giving you the best catalyst it can and you're still below the line.
items.tweetB: Equities up, 10y up 4bp to 5.11% on the same morning. That's not a risk-on rally, it's a supply rally: IPO money is coming out of bonds and the gains are going to Anthropic, not the index.

items.title: Quote of the day (Kun Chen): 'If AI is good at something, it will be infinitely replicated, so there's no scarcity'
items.idea: Bespoke opened with Kun Chen: 'If AI is good at something, it will be infinitely replicated, so there's no scarcity hence you can't really expect a sustainable business by creating anything with AI.'
items.angle: This is the bear case for the application layer ($IGV), and it explains why Pinkert shorts software while the market pays a premium for scarce inputs (compute, memory, power).
items.tweetA: 'AI makes everything infinitely replicable, so nothing built with AI is scarce.' Then the value goes to what can't be replicated: power, memory, fabs and trust. Sony can't build enough PlayStations because memory is the scarce part.
items.tweetB: Applying Kun Chen's line to the IPO: Anthropic sells something that gets replicated (inference) and buys something scarce (compute, $900B of it). The market just priced which side of that trade it thinks wins.

items.title: Capital Flows: SPX 7,400 is the line in the sand through the ANT IPO; by afternoon ES had flushed to 7,227
items.idea: Morning: a weekly close below 7,400 skews equities lower against 'significant cyclical headwinds'. Below it he runs tactical shorts; above it, neutral to tactical longs. He says we've shifted OUT of a credit-cycle melt-up and INTO wider ranges, aggressive rotations and positioning unwinds. Afternoon update: 'likely at a short term intraweek low in ES after we have flushed a lot of positioning post IPO. currently 7227.'
items.angle: ES is ~2.3% under his line. If Friday closes below 7,400, his framework says tactical shorts, even with the intraweek bounce he expects.
items.tweetA: ES opened the day above 7,400 and hit 7,227 by the afternoon. The IPO acted as the 'sell the news' event for the whole AI trade. One weekly close below 7,400 and the bounce becomes something to sell.
items.tweetB: 'Out of a credit-cycle melt-up, into positioning unwinds.' That's a regime call, not a trade. In unwinds, the most crowded longs fall first, and the most crowded long of 2026 just went public.

items.title: Anthropic priced at $83, above its $70–78 range; Amazon and Google own ~28%, and 7 companies buy a $26B private placement
items.idea: ANT priced at $83 per share and began trading on Nasdaq. Amazon and Google together own ~28% after the IPO; TipRanks puts Amazon's stake at ~$159B. Seven companies, including Alphabet and Microsoft, are buying $26B of stock in a private placement at the IPO price. GOOGL was +3.9% and AMZN +1.9% premarket; neoclouds CRWV +4.8% and IREN +4.3%.
items.angle: $AMZN now holds a ~$159B mark-to-market stake that will swing its reported earnings every quarter. $GOOGL and $MSFT buying at the IPO price looks like a circular-financing loop that will draw scrutiny.
items.tweetA: Amazon's Anthropic stake is worth ~$159B. That's a hyperscaler holding a stake larger than most S&P 500 companies in its biggest customer, which is also its competitor. Every ANT tick now runs through $AMZN's P&L.
items.tweetB: Seven companies, including Microsoft and Alphabet, put $26B into Anthropic at the IPO price. The suppliers are funding the customer that buys their compute. Nvidia did the same with its customers, and the market now discounts it.

items.title: Nvidia: Moody's cuts its outlook on CEO-succession risk; board approached Arm's Rene Haas; $500B in financing pledges, $0 deployed
items.idea: Moody's cut Nvidia's outlook to Stable from Positive (Aa1/P-1 affirmed), citing the leadership change and lack of a formal succession plan. Nvidia approached Arm CEO Rene Haas about replacing Jensen Huang (Bloomberg); some board members want Huang back (Semafor). Wall Street firms pledged ~$500B to help customers buy Nvidia chips, but the WSJ says none has been deployed. The Information reports Nvidia introduced Alibaba to alleged spy Alice Huang in 2022.
items.angle: Capital that's pledged but not deployed is optionality, not demand. If $500B of committed customer financing hasn't turned into orders, 2027 data-center guidance has an air pocket in it.
items.tweetA: Wall Street pledged $500B to help customers buy Nvidia chips, and the WSJ says $0 has been deployed. Pledged money is a press release. Deployed money is revenue. That gap is the real AI capex question.
items.tweetB: Moody's cut Nvidia's outlook because of key-man risk, not credit. The ratings agency is pricing the same thing Kyla wrote about: Nvidia was 'stacked on one person.' A move by Rene Haas from Arm to Nvidia would rewrite the CPU roadmap. $NVDA $ARM

items.title: Alibaba: AI cloud +53% to RMB 61B, but capex +60% and FCF of -RMB 34.5B; export controls weigh on next year's cloud guidance
items.idea: September-quarter revenue of RMB 271.5B (+10%) beat consensus of RMB 269.85B. Cloud and AI compute revenue rose 53% to RMB 61.0B, and adjusted EBITA was RMB 32.6B vs 9.1B. Capex rose 60% to RMB 50.5B, free cash flow was an outflow of RMB 34.5B, and the AI Labs loss widened to RMB 10.5B. Management said export-control uncertainty is tempering next year's cloud guidance; the stock fell premarket.
items.angle: China's AI capex math looks like the US version: capex (RMB 50.5B) nearly equals AI cloud revenue (RMB 61B). The difference is export controls cap the supply of chips, which tempers the guide. Same day, the US blocked Chinese remote access to advanced chips.
items.tweetA: Alibaba spent RMB 50.5B on capex to make RMB 61B of AI cloud revenue, and burned RMB 34.5B of FCF. That's China's version of the hyperscaler problem, with export controls tightening at the same time. $BABA
items.tweetB: AI cloud +53% in China, and management is still lowering next year's guide. The constraint isn't demand, it's chips. Washington just closed the remote-access route too. China's AI growth now depends on Huawei's fabs.

items.title: Calendar: Trump–Xi bilateral at APEC in Shenzhen, followed by a Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral
items.idea: SixSigma's morning brief lists a Trump–Xi bilateral at APEC in Shenzhen today, followed by a three-way Trump–Xi–Putin meeting. Crude was $83.38 (+1.81%).
items.angle: A three-way US–China–Russia summit while the US tightens chip access to China is a mixed signal. Oil at $83 is the variable most exposed to a Russia outcome.
items.tweetA: Trump, Xi and Putin are in one room in Shenzhen the same week the US blocks Chinese remote access to AI chips. The trilateral is about energy and Ukraine; the chips are the leverage.
items.tweetB: Crude is at $83 going into a Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral. Any Russia sanctions relief is a supply event the oil market isn't pricing.

items.title: Amazon warns NYC customers of up to $5 more per order if the delivery-worker bill passes; Uber Eats adds auto parts
items.idea: Amazon warned New York City customers they could pay up to $5 more per order if the city's delivery-worker bill passes (Reuters). Separately, Uber Eats launched an auto-parts category across ~7,000 US locations. Meta agreed not to issue non-voting Class C shares while the Zuckerberg share-plan suit proceeds; a Delaware trial is proposed for April.
items.angle: The cost of gig labor is now an explicit line on customer pricing. Amazon putting a number on it ($5) turns a labor bill into a consumer-price fight.
items.tweetA: Amazon told New Yorkers exactly what a delivery-worker law costs: $5 an order. Companies now pass labor regulation straight through to customers and let them lobby the city council.
items.tweetB: Uber Eats selling auto parts from ~7,000 stores. Same-day delivery is becoming the default for every retail category, which is exactly why the NYC labor bill matters to Amazon.

items.title: Quality plus Growth: why growth indexes ignore profitability, and QGRW's screen (48% IT)
items.idea: The S&P 500 Growth and Russell 1000 Growth indexes don't check profitability, debt or earnings stability, and quality indexes don't require growth. WisdomTree QGRW ranks the top 500 on 3-year average ROE/ROA plus forecast EPS growth, 5-year EBITA and sales growth, holds the top 100 cap-weighted, caps any holding at 15% and rebalances twice a year. Sector mix: IT 48.2%, Communication Services 15.0%, Consumer Discretionary 14.8%. TER 0.28% (UCITS 0.33%).
items.angle: A 'quality growth' screen that ends up 48% IT is mostly a mega-cap tech fund with a factor label, and it carries the same concentration risk Barclays flags for chips.
items.tweetA: A quality-growth ETF screens on ROE, ROA and growth and ends up 48% tech. In 2026, the factor screen and the momentum trade pick the same stocks. That's useful to know when momentum breaks.
items.tweetB: Growth indexes don't check profitability. Quality indexes don't check growth. Most investors own one of the two and think they're diversified.

items.title: A week of outages (Microsoft, FAA, Chase, NSA, Apple) may be AI-found exploits forcing mass patching
items.idea: Over five days: Microsoft products went down for about a day, the FAA ground-stopped every US flight for 4+ hours, Chase customers couldn't move money, and the NSA's classified network and Apple went down. Sen. Warner's explanation is that racing to patch dozens of AI-discovered exploits at once destabilized systems; Chris Krebs agreed. Nicole Perlroth says incident-response firms are backlogged six months. Rohit Krishnan notes five outages in five days also happened in early 2025.
items.angle: If AI finds bugs faster than humans can safely patch them, IT downtime becomes structural. That's bullish for cyber and observability vendors ($CRWD, $PANW, $DDOG) and for resilience spending.
items.tweetA: AI found the holes, everyone rushed to patch them, and the patches broke the systems. That's the most plausible explanation from the Senate Intelligence Committee. We've entered the era where AI's first real economic effect is a bill for downtime.
items.tweetB: Incident-response firms are backlogged six months. That's a capacity shortage in the one service you can't put off. Cyber pricing power is the clean read-through. $CRWD

items.title: Trust: only 9% of 18-34s have 'a great deal' of confidence in big companies; 48% have 'hardly any'
items.idea: WSJ/NORC: among 18–34 year olds, 9% have a great deal of confidence in major companies, 40% some and 48% hardly any; people 65+ trust more. Kyla's framework is saber vs conocer (knowing facts vs knowing people), built on Arrow's line that 'virtually every commercial transaction has within itself an element of trust,' Hayek's tacit knowledge and E.P. Thompson's moral economy. Her point is that the failure this week was the explanation, not the systems.
items.angle: Low institutional trust among young people is a long-run tailwind for decentralized, peer-to-peer and creator brands, and a headwind for incumbents' pricing power.
items.tweetA: 48% of 18–34s have 'hardly any' trust in big companies. That generation will be the biggest consumer cohort in a decade. Brands that sell on trust are losing their customers before they've won them.
items.tweetB: Kenneth Arrow, 1972: 'much of economic backwardness can be explained by the lack of mutual confidence.' Put that next to a 9% trust reading and you have a productivity story nobody models.

items.title: The FAA cut ~400 staff (132 rehired), and contractors now just notify the agency before touching radio sites
items.idea: Kyla details the FAA's February 2025 DOGE cuts (~400 people, mostly first-year staff and some maintenance mechanics; a judge restored 132). Since a March memo, contractors notify the FAA rather than asking permission. Sec. Duffy said it took a while to identify the router with L3Harris, the contractor that owns the network. A technician let a contractor swap a router in Arkansas and wasn't present while the work was done.
items.angle: Outsourced ownership of critical networks (L3Harris owns the FAA's) means the government depends on a contractor to diagnose its own outages. That supports federal IT modernization spending ($LHX, $LDOS, $BAH).
items.tweetA: The FAA had to ask its contractor which router broke, because the contractor owns the network. Outsourcing infrastructure means outsourcing the knowledge of how it works. $LHX
items.tweetB: Tacit knowledge doesn't show up on a balance sheet until it's gone. 268 FAA staff cut and not rehired, then a 4-hour national ground stop. Nobody has proven the link, and nobody can rule it out.

items.title: Anthropic's IPO: $81B raised, the biggest ever; $900B of compute planned through 2045; 90+ pages on existential risk
items.idea: Kyla: ANT raised $81B at $83, massively oversubscribed. The company plans to spend $900B on compute between now and 2045 ('bold but sane'), and the prospectus has 90+ pages on catastrophic or existential risk. A trust elects most of the board, so public shareholders get little say. Fast Nasdaq-100 entry is expected, so index funds will own it.
items.angle: Fast index inclusion turns passive money into the marginal buyer of a company whose governance limits shareholder voice. Expect $QQQ rebalance flows.
items.tweetA: $900B of compute through 2045 is roughly $47B a year for ~19 years, about 70% of Anthropic's current ~$68B run-rate, every year. And every Nasdaq-100 index fund will own it, with no vote.
items.tweetB: The first company with 90+ pages of existential-risk disclosure in its S-1 is about to sit in every retirement account by way of the Nasdaq-100. The risk factors are bigger than the float.

items.title: Memory shortage hits GTA VI: Sony can build ~10M consoles vs. 16–17M hoped
items.idea: FT via Kyla: Sony hoped to sell 16–17M consoles but memory prices and constraints cap it at ~10M. Analyst Robin Zhu: 'Constraints on memory supply and cost mean Sony is unlikely to be able to scale production to take full advantage of GTA-driven demand.' GTA VI launched the same day ANT began trading.
items.angle: AI's demand for HBM and DRAM is crowding out consumer electronics. It's bullish for $MU, SK Hynix and Samsung pricing, and bearish for console, PC and phone unit volumes.
items.tweetA: Sony will build ~40% fewer PlayStations than it wanted during the biggest game launch in history, because AI is buying all the memory. The AI buildout is now taking the console market's memory supply. $MU $SONY
items.tweetB: GTA VI and Anthropic debuted the same day, and they're competing for the same DRAM. Anthropic is winning.

items.title: Voters across parties want 'fairness, not free stuff,' and El-Sayed and Rob Sand won by speaking 'truth to pain'
items.idea: A WSJ poll found majorities across party lines want action on surprise medical bills, insurer denials, drug prices, credit card rates, institutional buyers of single-family homes and childcare costs, but not government grocery stores or $5,000 checks. A GOP pollster: 'Every popular item... has someone standing between you and a fair price.' Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's Senate seat; Rob Sand won the Iowa governor's race after 200+ town halls.
items.angle: Bipartisan support for policies targeting middlemen means regulatory risk for PBMs, insurers ($UNH, $CVS), card issuers (rate caps) and single-family rental REITs ($INVH, $AMH).
items.tweetA: The new bipartisan consensus isn't left or right, it's anti-middleman. Insurers, PBMs, card issuers and SFR landlords all appear on the same poll. That's a sector short list, not a political story.
items.tweetB: Voters don't want $5,000 checks. They want to know the price in advance. Price transparency is the most popular economic policy in America, and nobody has priced what it does to margins.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (DB India)
items.title: Deutsche Bank: the AI winners may be adopters like India, not builders; FPIs bought a record $9.5B of India in November
items.idea: Adrian Cox (DB Research Institute) argues the economic winners of AI may be economies that adopt cheap, powerful AI across huge populations rather than those funding frontier models. India has ~1.5B potential users, a young workforce, an IT-services base and digital public infrastructure. Foreign investors bought a record $9.5B of Indian equities in November after selling ~$26B in the first nine months of 2026, as crowded US and North Asia AI trades unwound.
items.angle: India works as the anti-AI-capex hedge: it benefits from falling model costs without the capex. Watch $INDA vs $SMH. Indian IT services face the adjustment, but domestic consumption gains.
items.tweetA: Foreign money dumped $26B of India in 9 months, then bought a record $9.5B in one. As the AI-builder trade unwinds, the AI-adopter trade gets bid. India owns no frontier model and doesn't need one.
items.tweetB: Model prices fall every quarter (Gemini 4 Neon at $3/M tokens). Whoever doesn't pay for the capex gets the deflation for free. The US and China build it, India uses it. $INDA

charts.desc: Monthly FPI flows into Indian equities, with the record November bar after nine months of selling. 🔥

items.title: Danny Dayan's 'The Miracle': is the AI productivity payoff showing up just as the market sours on AI infra?
items.idea: Dayan frames the premise: AI raises productivity, which pulls more workflows onto AI and pays off the capex. He asks whether the productivity 'miracle' is surfacing in the data right as the market turns on the infrastructure trade, and calls the note 'very important' with large macro and micro implications. The email is a teaser; the full analysis is paywalled.
items.angle: If productivity data inflects while the capex trade sells off, the rotation is from AI builders to AI users. That's the same conclusion as DB's India note from the macro side.
items.tweetA: The market is selling AI infrastructure just as productivity data may be turning up. That's how capex cycles end: the builders get hurt and the users collect the gains.
items.tweetB: If the productivity 'miracle' is real, it's disinflationary, and Waller is hiking into it. A 50bp hike just as productivity accelerates would be a textbook policy error.

items.title: Big BTC miners are leaving for AI. The ones who stay may benefit, and 100% bonus depreciation makes rigs a tax play
items.idea: Beau Turner (Abundant Mines) explains why he's staying in BTC mining while large miners convert to AI data centers or leave altogether. Fewer competitors means a bigger hashprice share for those who remain. He argues ASIC obsolescence is less of a problem than it used to be, and pitches mining rigs as a year-end tax shelter under 100% bonus depreciation.
items.angle: Hashrate leaving for AI is a supply-side tailwind for pure-play miners' margins. The 100% bonus-depreciation demand for rigs could pull ASIC orders into Q4.
items.tweetA: Miners leaving BTC for AI is the best thing to happen to the miners who stay. Difficulty adjusts down, hashprice share goes up. AI is subsidizing the bitcoin miners who refuse to switch.
items.tweetB: Buying mining rigs for 100% bonus depreciation in December is a tax trade, not a bitcoin trade. Expect a Q4 bump in ASIC demand that disappears in January.

items.title: Strive's Matt Cole is 'happy to pay a 15% dividend forever' on SATS; STRC/SATA fell into the $70s–80s this summer
items.idea: Strive CEO Matt Cole (16 years at CalPERS, ~$70B managed) will pay 15% on the new SATS preferred 'forever', betting BTC appreciates far more while the dollars paid out lose value. Digital-credit products like STRC and SATA traded down to the $70s–80s during the summer volatility, with leverage and margin calls involved. He frames the preferreds as a way around institutional mandates that can't hold BTC directly. Saylor and Phong Le do a Q3 investor Q&A today.
items.angle: A 15% perpetual coupon vs a 5.11% 10y is a ~990bp spread, priced like distressed debt. It's sustainable only if BTC compounds above ~15% a year in dollars.
items.tweetA: A 15% perpetual dividend when the 10y pays 5.11%. That's ~990bp over Treasuries, high-yield-distressed pricing on a company whose only asset is bitcoin. The coupon is the market's real read on BTC risk.
items.tweetB: STRC and SATA traded in the $70s this summer. That was the stress test, and they failed it. Now BTC is under $63k with RSI below 20. Watch the preferreds, not BTC: they break first.

items.source: Running of the Bulltards / James Bulltard
items.title: Bulltard: bearish engulfing at SPY's 200-DMA, QQQ over a month below its 21-EMA, 'if you're not in all cash yet, think about it'
items.idea: SPY gapped back above its 200-day on the ANT debut but faded into a bearish engulfing candle at the 200-DMA, without touching the 8-EMA. QQQ faded a 500-point move and has been below its 21-EMA for over a month. Every moving average is sloping down. He expects thin volume into Thanksgiving and doesn't see where a Santa rally comes from in 2026.
items.angle: Technicians on both sides (Bulltard, Capital Flows, Pinkert) agree the IPO bounce failed. The difference is timing: Capital Flows sees a short-term low at 7,227.
items.tweetA: The biggest IPO in history printed a bearish engulfing candle on the S&P's 200-DMA. Markets don't usually give you a cleaner 'sell the news' signal than that.
items.tweetB: Three independent tape readers today (a CMT, a macro chat and a trend follower) all say the ANT bounce failed. When technicians who usually disagree agree, the trade gets crowded fast. Capital Flows' call for a short-term low is the contrarian one.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes (Barclays 2027)
items.title: Barclays joins Goldman and Morgan Stanley at exactly 8,700 SPX for 2027, with earnings growth leaning heavily on chips
items.idea: Venu Krishna's 2027 Outlook, 'Chips and Dips,' sees another year of strong earnings growth and buying opportunities in the correction, but semiconductors carry an extraordinary share of expected S&P earnings growth. GS, MS and Barclays all land on 8,700 by different routes (different EPS, rate and AI-winner assumptions). Financing needs and the search for measurable AI returns are getting harder to ignore.
items.angle: From ES at 7,227, 8,700 is ~+20%. Consensus that tidy, with earnings concentrated in the most cyclical industry, is a fragility signal.
items.tweetA: Goldman 8,700. Morgan Stanley 8,700. Barclays 8,700. Three different models, one number. That's not three forecasts, it's one consensus. And the earnings behind it depend on chips, while Moody's is downgrading Nvidia's outlook.
items.tweetB: 8,700 is +20% from ES 7,227, and most of the EPS growth is semis. Look at NVDA guidance: it's a single-sector bet presented as an index target.

items.title: BNY and Microsoft had two AI agents negotiate a US Treasury trade, and repo is next
items.idea: Two agents exchanged offers and counteroffers within approved pricing limits; human traders then reviewed and completed the trade, which they call an industry first. Bloomberg saw the transcript and noted the agents were 'unusually polite.' BNY plans tests beyond two-party deals and possibly repo. Tradeweb is extending its AI assistant to government bonds with ~a dozen firms testing it.
items.angle: Agent-to-agent negotiation in the deepest market in the world is the start of machine-speed OTC. It's a long-run margin squeeze for voice dealers and a tailwind for $TW.
items.tweetA: The first Treasury trade negotiated agent-to-agent happened this week, and the agents were more polite than the traders. Next up is repo, the $4T+ plumbing of the financial system.
items.tweetB: The same week BNY's agents negotiated a Treasury trade, Fed Governor Barr warned that AI agents can learn to collude without talking. Those two stories collide in a bond market run by agents.

items.title: Fed's Barr: AI herding, tacit agent collusion and agent-driven bank runs; AI is now the top-cited risk in the Fed's stability survey
items.idea: Barr (ICAIF Milan) warned that firms using the same models could hold the same positions and amplify downturns. He cited research showing agents learn to collude without communicating, and said agents moving deposits quickly could make bank funding more volatile and that banks see agents acting in accounts without verified consent. The Fed's semiannual Financial Stability Report found AI is the most-cited risk among 23 market contacts. APRA plans a 2027 AI-disruption stress test.
items.angle: Agent-driven deposit flight is SVB at machine speed. It's a reason for higher bank liquidity requirements, which hurts regional bank ROE ($KRE).
items.tweetA: SVB lost $42B in a day with humans on phones. Barr is warning about deposits that move at agent speed. Regional banks' funding models assume deposits are slow. That assumption has an expiry date.
items.tweetB: The Fed's stability survey now names AI as the #1 risk, ahead of everything else. Australia will stress-test AI disruption in 2027. Regulators are pricing AI as a systemic risk before the market prices it as a cyclical one.

items.title: Rogo nears $3.75B on $77M ARR (from $41M in June), with negative margins getting worse; Model ML raises $250M at $1.5B
items.idea: Rogo (AI agents for banker modeling and deal work) is raising ~$350M at $3.75B, nearly double April's valuation, led by Bessemer and General Catalyst. ARR went from $41M at end-June to $77M at end-October, but Bloomberg says rising model costs deepened its negative margins. Model ML raised $250M at $1.5B (General Atlantic, QED), with ~$60M under contract by year-end.
items.angle: Thin AI apps carry a negative gross-margin problem: they grow ARR but pay the model vendors. Value goes to the model layer (ANT) until inference prices fall.
items.tweetA: Rogo: ARR +88% in four months, valued at ~49x ARR, and margins getting more negative as it grows. Every dollar of revenue sends more than a dollar to the model provider. That's a reseller, not a SaaS company.
items.tweetB: Anthropic IPOs the same week its customers report worsening margins from 'rising costs to run AI models.' One company's revenue is the other company's negative gross margin.

items.title: Agents get wallets: ChatGPT Wallet buys with Face ID approval; Gemini gets read-only bank access via Plaid; KPMG ran a 100-agent audit
items.idea: OpenAI's ChatGPT Wallet (Nov. 13) lets agents make purchases with per-purchase approval and without sharing card details, with spending limits as the eventual goal. Google connected Gemini to Google Wallet with read-only Plaid access for budgets and forgotten subscriptions. KPMG UK's audit head said an experiment with 100+ AI agents reviewing a listed company's accounts 'was able to go so much deeper.'
items.angle: Agentic commerce runs through the card networks and tokenization ($V, $MA, $PYPL), and Plaid is the data rail. Audit automation compresses Big 4 junior labor.
items.tweetA: ChatGPT can now spend your money with a Face ID tap, and Gemini can read every bank account you link. The checkout page, the last thing between you and an impulse buy, is being automated away.
items.tweetB: 100 AI agents audited a listed company's books and went 'so much deeper' than humans. The audit pyramid (thousands of juniors ticking boxes) is the next white-collar labor market to reprice.

items.title: Variational: 32% of supply to its first airdrop, which at $1.5B FDV is ~$480M, the biggest airdrop of 2026
items.idea: Variational is the 3rd-largest perps DEX by volume and the most popular DEX without a token. After its $110M Series B at $1.5B, the team committed 32% of supply to the first airdrop, ~$480M at that FDV. The author farms it with delta-neutral funding-rate arbitrage vs Hyperliquid (screen via Bendbasis, >15% APR, >$150k OI, FDV over $500M, 2–2.5x cross margin, close when the spread is negative for several hours).
items.angle: Points farming via funding arb inflates reported volume. Perp DEX volume rankings now include a lot of airdrop wash flow.
items.tweetA: 32% of supply × $1.5B = a $480M airdrop. The catch: farmers using delta-neutral funding arb are generating much of the volume. Discount 'volume' for perps DEXs that haven't launched a token yet.
items.tweetB: VCs paid $1.5B for Variational knowing 32% goes to farmers. They're betting the token launches above $1.5B. In this tape, that's a bet on a recovery by TGE.

items.title: Bitcoin's daily RSI dropped below 20
items.idea: Chart of the week: BTC daily RSI fell below 20 (blocmates: BTC under $63k, talk of $50–59k). Also in the DeFi roundup: xStocks launches tokenized Anthropic shares on Mantle today; Hyperliquid perps integrated into Bitso (LatAm's largest crypto app); Solana Foundation became majority investor in CoinGecko; Frax buys back and burns with revenue; CFTC approved Backpack's perps platform.
items.angle: A daily RSI below 20 is rare oversold territory. It usually gives a reflexive bounce, but not necessarily a bottom. Strive and STRC preferreds are the stress point to watch.
items.tweetA: BTC's daily RSI is under 20. In past cycles that's marked capitulation lows more often than not. But it's also where forced sellers (preferreds, miners, treasuries) get margin calls. Watch $MSTR, not the chart.
items.tweetB: Tokenized Anthropic stock went live on Mantle the same day as the Nasdaq listing, while BTC printed RSI < 20. Crypto rails are winning the tokenization race while the native asset sinks.

items.title: Disney's 5th earnings triple play in 12 quarters, back near the $125 ceiling that's held for 4 years; would build cruise ships faster
items.idea: DIS fell 1.48% on earnings day, then rallied 4.63%, to within 2.1% of its August 2022 closing high of $124.96. Prior rallies stalled at $122.82 (Apr 2024) and $124.01 (Jun 2025). It's up 32% from the March low. US park attendance +3% and per-guest spending +4% (ex extra week). CEO Josh D'Amaro said Disney would add cruise ships faster if they could be built to its standards. August was Marvel's biggest month ever on Disney+ ahead of Avengers: Doomsday on Dec. 18.
items.angle: Experiential spending (parks, cruises) is holding up while consumer trust sits at a low. Shipyard capacity, not demand, is the cruise constraint, which also helps $RCL and $CCL pricing.
items.tweetA: Disney says it would add cruise ships faster if anyone could build them. In a market selling everything, the bottleneck in leisure is shipyards, not consumers. $DIS $RCL
items.tweetB: Third try at $125 in four years, with a 32% run from March. Breakouts through levels tested this often tend to run. Avengers on Dec. 18 is the catalyst on the calendar.

items.title: Robert Sinn: junior miners are in capitulation ('just make it stop'), even FCX, ALB and CCJ; next comes despondency, the max-opportunity stage
items.idea: After three months of nonstop selling, this week's price and volume action 'feels a lot like October 2008 or March 2020.' Sinn shows capitulation in Freeport, Albemarle and Cameco. Next is despondency, 'the point of maximum financial opportunity,' but juniors can stay weak for weeks after metals and majors bottom, especially in tax-loss season. His Tax Loss list comes Dec. 1. 'Don't use margin and don't let your cash balance reach zero.'
items.angle: Capitulation in $FCX, $ALB and $CCJ at once, across copper, lithium and uranium, suggests a macro (dollar, Waller) liquidation rather than sector fundamentals. That's the setup for a January rebound in juniors ($GDXJ, $SIL).
items.tweetA: Copper, lithium and uranium are all capitulating in the same week. Those don't share fundamentals. They share a dollar at its highest since April 2025. When everything with a ticker in the ground falls together, it's a liquidity event.
items.tweetB: Tax-loss selling in juniors runs into late December, then stops on Jan. 1. That's the most dependable calendar trade in resources, and this year it starts from 2008-style capitulation.

items.title: Crypto traded ANT before Nasdaq did: trade[XYZ] and Lighter had pre-IPO Anthropic at or above $83
items.idea: Anthropic named Nasdaq as its venue, but trade[XYZ] and Lighter already had pre-IPO ANT trading around and above $83. Wall Street analyst targets sit 81% above the IPO price. Separately, the Center for AI Safety published 'The MisAnthropic Statement,' a coalition accusing Anthropic of racing to build the recursively self-improving AI it warns about.
items.angle: Onchain pre-IPO price discovery for the biggest IPO ever is a proof point for perp DEXs and tokenized equities (Hyperliquid HIP-3, xStocks).
items.tweetA: The biggest IPO in history found its price on a crypto perp DEX before the Nasdaq bell. Onchain markets didn't just track ANT; they priced it first.
items.tweetB: Analyst targets 81% above the IPO price, and a safety coalition publishing a 'MisAnthropic Statement' on listing day. The bull and bear cases on ANT both arrived before the stock had a closing price.

items.title: Anthropic: $0 revenue in Q1 2023, $17B in Q3 2026 (+1,127% YoY); Nvidia Q3 $115.8B, 93% data center
items.idea: blocmates: Anthropic went from $0 in Q1 2023 to $17B in Q3 2026 revenue, up 1,127% YoY. Nvidia's Q3 revenue was $115.8B, 93% from data centers. In model news, OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra is the first externally deployed model to meet OpenAI's 'High' threshold for AI self-improvement; Gemini 4 Neon scores 63.7% on CursorBench 4.1 at $3 per million input tokens; Qwen4-Max has 1M context.
items.angle: $17B a quarter is a ~$68B run-rate. That's a customer that now matters for Nvidia, Google TPUs and Amazon Trainium allocations.
items.tweetA: Anthropic did $17B in Q3. That's a $68B run-rate, around 15% of Nvidia's own quarterly revenue in a single quarter, from a company that had zero revenue three years ago.
items.tweetB: OpenAI just shipped the first model that meets its own 'High' self-improvement threshold, the same week Anthropic IPO'd with 90 pages of existential-risk disclosure. The safety debate has become a 10-K disclosure question.

items.title: Wells Fargo doubles its IBIT stake to 30,553 BTC and becomes the largest institutional BTC ETF holder; BitMine holds 4.97% of ETH
items.idea: blocmates roundup: Wells Fargo doubled its IBIT position to 30,553 BTC, now the biggest institutional Bitcoin ETF holder. BitMine holds 6,077,745 ETH (4.97% of supply) after buying 7,653 more. Aave V4 passed $1.75B in deposits; Lighter has bought back 20M LIT (8% of circulating); Aptos burned 2.1M APT since mainnet.
items.angle: A bulge-bracket wirehouse doubling into the drawdown is real-money accumulation while retail flows (XRP ETFs) exit.
items.tweetA: BTC under $63k, RSI under 20, XRP ETFs bleeding, and Wells Fargo doubles to 30,553 BTC (~$1.9B). Retail is capitulating and the wirehouses are buying.
items.tweetB: BitMine is at 4.97% of all ETH and still buying while staking yields fall to 2.2%. A single treasury approaching 5% of supply is a concentration risk the ETH market hasn't priced.

items.title: Hackers hijacked ~64,000 BTC mining machines, pointed 13 EH/s at OCEAN, and mined zero blocks
items.idea: blocmates: attackers hijacked about 64,000 mining machines and redirected 13 EH/s to the OCEAN pool, but mined no blocks. Same week: wallet-swapping malware was slipped into 178 websites, Ledger's among them; Lighter paused withdrawals over a leaked API key (the attacker moved funds to Hyperliquid to buy Monero); Google says 'the era of autonomous attacks has arrived' and the FBI warns of an AI-powered tool that automates attacks.
items.angle: Fleet-level ASIC compromise is a new attack class, both a hashrate-security issue and an opex risk for miners. It ties directly to the AI-automated attack warnings.
items.tweetA: 64,000 hijacked mining rigs and 13 EH/s stolen, and the hackers mined zero blocks. Even crime has variance risk. The real story is that miners' fleets can be taken over remotely at scale.
items.tweetB: Google: 'the era of autonomous attacks has arrived.' Same week: 64k mining rigs hijacked, 178 websites trojaned, a US-wide outage cluster. Cyber has gone from an IT line item to a macro variable.

items.title: A single HIP-3 deployer accounts for 50% of Hyperliquid's volume
items.idea: blocmates notes one HIP-3 (builder-deployed perps) deployer is responsible for half of Hyperliquid's volume. Hyperliquid's HIP-4 outcome markets are also gaining, led by Outcome (500k staked HYPE requirement met). LayerV points out options volume is holding up while spot, perps and futures volumes fall.
items.angle: Half of the volume from one deployer is a concentration risk for $HYPE's fee base. If that deployer leaves or blows up, reported volume halves.
items.tweetA: 50% of Hyperliquid's volume comes from one HIP-3 deployer. That makes it a platform with one huge customer, not a decentralized exchange. $HYPE
items.tweetB: Spot, perps and futures volumes are falling and options are holding up. Traders are paying for convexity instead of direction. That's what crypto looks like near a vol regime change.

items.title: SCOTUS declines Custodia's master-account case; South Korea allows bank-majority won stablecoins; Solana drops 'beta'
items.idea: The Supreme Court declined Custodia Bank's master-account case, leaving regional Fed banks free to say no. South Korea lets tech companies launch won stablecoins, with banks holding majority ownership. Solana formally left mainnet 'beta' after seven years. Coinbase opened USDC borrowing against BTC/ETH/SOL in all 50 states via Morpho on Base; the CFTC approved Backpack's US derivatives exchange.
items.angle: Without a Fed master account, crypto banks stay dependent on correspondent banks. Korea's bank-majority model is the opposite design choice from GENIUS's state-charter debate.
items.tweetA: The Supreme Court won't hear Custodia, so the Fed can keep crypto banks off its payment rails indefinitely. Meanwhile Korea forces banks to own the stablecoin issuers. Two models for one question: who owns the dollar (or won) API?
items.tweetB: Solana dropped 'beta' after seven years, in a quarter where SOL-backed loans went live in all 50 states. The infrastructure is graduating faster than the price.

items.title: XRP drops as low as $0.89, down 36% this quarter, with the biggest weekly ETF outflow since March; BTC below $63k
items.idea: blocmates: BTC fell below $63k in 48 hours, with speculation about $50–59k, and attention shifting to Pearl (useful-AI-work mining; Kairos put its biggest Pearl upgrade on testnet). XRP hit $0.89, down 36% QTD, as XRP ETFs logged their biggest weekly outflow since March. Their joke: buying BTC instead of GTA V 13 years ago would be up more than 48,000%.
items.angle: ETF wrappers make alt-coin outflows visible and pro-cyclical. Pearl/AI-useful mining is an emerging narrative competitor to BTC's energy story.
items.tweetA: XRP is down 36% this quarter and the ETFs are seeing record outflows. ETFs brought alts new buyers, and they also made every exit a public, daily number.
items.tweetB: BTC below $63k while the AI trade unwinds, and the conversation shifts to 'useful work' mining (Pearl). The bitcoin-as-energy-sink story is losing to AI for the same megawatts.

items.title: US blocks China from remotely accessing advanced AI chips; White House weighs forcing disclosure of Chinese model use
items.idea: blocmates AI roundup: the US blocked China from remotely accessing advanced AI chips (closing the cloud-rental route), and the White House is weighing rules that would make companies disclose any use of Chinese AI models. Alibaba cited export-control uncertainty in its guide the same morning.
items.angle: Closing remote access hurts neoclouds with Chinese demand and helps domestic Chinese silicon (Huawei Ascend, SMIC). Disclosure rules would be a compliance cost for anyone using Qwen or DeepSeek.
items.tweetA: The cloud loophole is closed: China can't rent US AI chips remotely anymore. Alibaba lowered its cloud guide the same morning. Every Chinese AI dollar now goes to Huawei.
items.tweetB: If US companies must disclose using Chinese AI models, Qwen4-Max's 1M context and 50% token savings become a compliance liability. That's a tariff on cheap inference.

items.title: Haymaker: most commodities are in deficit yet falling all year (ex-oil), with the 'wrecking ball dollar' doing damage again
items.idea: Haymaker Daily: 'Commodity prices have been under pressure for most of the year, outside of oil. This is despite the reality that most are in a supply deficit.' The headline is 'Wrecking Ball Dollar Wreaking Havoc (Again).' The rest is paywalled.
items.angle: A deficit with falling prices means financial selling, driven by the dollar. If the DXY tops (Pinkert is probing for one), the deficit reasserts itself fast.
items.tweetA: Supply deficit plus falling price equals a dollar problem, not a commodity problem. The day the DXY turns, all the deficits Goldman and Haymaker have been writing about get repriced at once.
items.tweetB: Oil is the only commodity up this year, and it's the one with a geopolitical premium. Everything that trades on fundamentals is losing to the dollar.

items.title: Imbue's Kanjun Qiu: the AI industry mood is 'uncertain and somewhat melancholy'; maybe humans aren't 'output machines'
items.idea: Qiu's diagnosis: 100+ years of industrialization taught people their purpose was output. As AI takes the grunt work, people may gain a sense of authorship over their lives. The episode also covers odds on Huang returning to Nvidia (Huang posted 'I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO'), Brad Gerstner aiming to put $5B into the ANT IPO, Chamath's 'ALL existing software needs to be rewritten,' Bill Gurley on 'handoverism,' and whether the outage cluster was coincidence or attack.
items.angle: When the builders describe the mood as melancholy on the day of the biggest AI IPO, sentiment inside the industry is out of step with the price action. That's a culture signal worth tracking.
items.tweetA: On the day of the biggest IPO in history, an AI founder calls the industry mood 'melancholy.' The people building it feel worse than the people buying it. That's usually an early signal.
items.tweetB: Gerstner wants $5B of ANT at the IPO, and Chamath says ALL software must be rewritten. If they're right, $IGV isn't cheap. The software rewrite is a capex cycle disguised as a disruption story.
